sources.citation: Li Jinfang & Luo Yongxian. 2010. The Buyang language of South China: grammatical notes, glossary, texts and translations. Pacific Linguistics 607. Canberra: ANU (open access, CC BY-SA 4.0, handle 1885/146755).
sources.note: Describes PAHA (Baha) Buyang of Guangnan [baha1256], not Yerong. Sect. 2.1.5 Tones (pp. 10-11): seven tones, complex tone sandhi, some prefixes carry a neutral tone (0), likened to sesquisyllabic Austroasiatic word shapes. The words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur anywhere in the book. Intro (p. 2) classifies Buyang into an Eastern Group (Napo, 'represented by Yarong'; Langjia; E'ma) and a Western Group (Paha).

sources.citation: Schiering, René & Harry van der Hulst. 2010. Word accent systems in the languages of Asia. In van der Hulst, Goedemans & van Zanten (eds), A Survey of Word Accentual Patterns in the Languages of the World, 509-599. De Gruyter Mouton.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, paywalled at the publisher
sources.note: Sect. 7.4 Tai-Kadai lists 'BU-RONG: Yerong' in the genetic tree (p. 597) but the accent information (p. 598) is family-level only: 'All languages in this family are tonal and morphemes are monosyllabic', followed by Thai and Lao final-stress remarks; nothing on Yerong specifically.
sources.venue: A Survey of Word Accentual Patterns in the Languages of the World

sources.citation: Ostapirat, Weera. 2000. Proto-Kra. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 23(1): 1-251.
sources.note: Comparative reconstruction; scan without text, pp. 1-30 scanned. Buyang data are from the E-Cun (representative) and Langjia dialects (p. 5), i.e. E'ma/Langnian, not Yerong. No stress statement in the scanned introduction; only tone categories A/B/C/D.

sources.citation: Li Jingfang & Zhou Guoyan. 1998. Diachronic evolution of initial consonants in Buyang. Mon-Khmer Studies 28: 115-135.
sources.note: Historical study of initials comparing Baha, Yalang (= Yerong [yrn]), Ecun and Langjia; tone letters given on forms; nothing on stress (pp. 115-117 scanned, rest skimmed as scan).

sources.citation: Li Jinfang. 1996. The sound system of Baha Buyang. In Pan-Asiatic Linguistics: Proceedings of the Fourth International Symposium on Languages and Linguistics, 141-150. Mahidol University.
sources.note: Baha, not Yerong. Sect. 3 Tones (p. 149): 'Baha has 7 tones.. Some prefixes are pronounced with a light tone 0'. No stress/accent statement. Its reference list cites Li Jinfang 1995b 'Yalhong — a dialect of Buyang language (to be published in Kadai)', the earliest description of the Napo (Yerong) dialect; no published copy located.

sources.citation: Wikipedia (en) 'Buyang language' and 'Yerong language'; Wikipedia (zh) 布央语; Glottolog 5.1 languoid page yero1238; ISO 639-3 page yrn.
sources.note: Yerong = southern Buyang, Rongtun village near Longhe Township, Napo County, Guangxi, c. 300-400 speakers; Glottolog alternative names Yalang Buyang 雅郎布央, 耶容布央, Daban Yao, 六瑶/土瑶/铁瑶. No tone or stress information for Yerong on any of these pages.

sources.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. 2008. Kra or Kadai languages. In A. Diller, J. Edmondson & Y. Luo (eds), The Tai-Kadai Languages, 653-677. London: Routledge.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: This work describes Kra (Kadai) group overview: Gelao (Wanzi, Pingba, Laozhai, Qiaoshang, Red Gelao Na Khe, White Gelao, Sanchong), Laha (Noong Lay and Ta Mit, first-hand), Buyang (Paha, Yalang, Ecun, Langjia, data from Li Jinfang); Lachi and Qabiao get one pa. No statement of Yalang's tone inventory, stress or accent anywhere in the chapter; Yalang occurs only as tone-numbered forms (digits seen: 53, 12, 33, 31) in comparative tables. sources.note: The reprint's Google Books snippet reads '耶容话与安顺仡佬语比较接近,声母、韵母、声调都有对应,但声母的对应关系没有韵母、声调那样复杂' (Yerong is close to Anshun Gelao; initials, rhymes and tones all correspond), and 中国现代语言学家传略 (2004) says the article 'generally describes the components of the language and its structural type' besides arguing affiliation - i.e. a 概况-style sketch with a 声韵调 (initial/rhyme/tone) inventory of Rongtun Yerong plus Yerong-Gelao tone correspondences. Number and values of the tones not seen in snippet.

sources.note: Google Books snippets from ch. 2 sect. 3 (En vs Buyang): '..调 53。郎架布央语有 6 个声调:平调 33,升调 24,中降调 31,低降调 312,高平调 54,低平调 11。与台语、侗水语相比,仡央语言及方言间声调的对应很不整齐.. 以下我们列出恩语和雅郎、郎架布央语声调对应的大致情形,但每一种对应都有不少例外的词。郎架 33 调大多出现在壮语借词,与恩语、雅郎话没对应关系' - i.e. tone inventories per dialect (the Yalang inventory immediately precedes the snippet, ending in a 53 tone) followed by En-Yalang-Langjia tone-correspondence sets; the appendix wordlist gives Yalang forms with tone values.
